title: Middle-aged mice treated with GHK-Cu peptide administered intraperitoneally or intranasally show behavioral rescue but divergent hippocampal aging programs

citation.title: Middle-aged mice treated with GHK-Cu peptide administered intraperitoneally or intranasally show behavioral rescue but divergent hippocampal aging programs

printed_heading.text: Middle-aged mice treated with GHK-Cu peptide administered intraperitoneally or intranasally show behavioral rescue but divergent hippocampal aging programs Jordan Mazzola University of Washington Manuela Rosenfeld University of Washington Matthew Tucker University of Washington Jackson Wezeman University of Washington Warren Ladiges University of Washington Gerald Liao University of Washington Article Keywords: aging, cognitive decline, GHK-Cu peptide, intraperitoneal delivery, intranasal delivery, RNA sequencing Posted Date: May 26th, 2026 DOI: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-9520102/v1 License:   This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. what_it_measured.text: Molecular effects were evaluated using hippocampal immunohistochemistry and bulk RNA sequencing.
Hippocampaldependent escape learning was assessed using a spatial navigation task.

dose.text: Aged C57BL/6J mice (20–21 months) received GHK-Cu (15 mg/kg) via short-term intraperitoneal (IP; 5 days) or longer-term intranasal (IN; 8 weeks) administration.
GHK was administered as a copper complex (GHK-Cu; Active Peptide, Cambridge, MA) at 15 mg/kg, selected based on efficacy and safety relative to known copper toxicity thresholds [20–21].

route.text: Aged C57BL/6J mice (20–21 months) received GHK-Cu (15 mg/kg) via short-term intraperitoneal (IP; 5 days) or longer-term intranasal (IN; 8 weeks) administration.

endpoint.text: Differential gene expression was analyzed using DESeq2 with false discovery rate (FDR) correction, and pathway-level changes were assessed via gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA).
Molecular effects were evaluated using hippocampal immunohistochemistry and bulk RNA sequencing.
Hippocampaldependent escape learning was assessed using a spatial navigation task.

reported_results.text: IN treatment increased synaptophysin in females (P < 0.001) and decreased GFAP in both sexes (P < 0.01), while IP treatment reduced TGF-β, GFAP, and MCP-1 in males (P < 0.05) and decreased p21 in females (P < 0.0001).

IN GHK-Cu improved escape latency across Trials 2–4 in both sexes (P < 0.05), whereas IP dosing produced a transient improvement in males during Trial 2 (P < 0.05) without sustained effects or improvement in females.
Short-term IP dosing decreased TGF-β, GFAP, and MCP-1 in the male hippocampus (P’s < 0.05) (Figs. 3A-C). p21 expression decreased in the female hippocampus (P < 0.0001) (Fig. 3D).
In the hippocampus, IN treatment increased synaptophysin in females (P < 0.001) (Fig. 2A), while both sexes demonstrated modulation of GFAP (P’s < 0.01) (Fig. 2B).

In contrast, short-term IP dosing (5 days) improved escape latency in males during Trial 2 (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1C) but did not sustain improvement through Trials 3–4 and did not improve performance in females (P’s > 0.05) (Fig. 1C-D).
IN GHK-Cu (8 weeks) improved escape performance in both sexes following initial exposure, with reduced escape latency across Trials 2–4 (P’s < 0.05) (Fig. 1A-B).
